quests.instruction: Which two features are heard in “Bella, ask for it at once”?
quests.word: Bella, ask for it at once
quests.textToSpeak: Bella, ask for it at once
options: A strong “for” with a clear break after “ask”, and no link before “it”
Elision of the /k/ in “ask”, and a strong “it” that keeps its own beat
A weak “for” that takes the /k/ of “ask”, and a linking /r/ before “it”
Assimilation of the /k/ to /f/ before “for”, with a clear /r/ afterwards
quests.correctAnswer: A weak “for” that takes the /k/ of “ask”, and a linking /r/ before “it”
quests.hint: Look at the small word between “ask” and “it”. What happens to its vowel, and what links to it?
quests.explanation: “For” is a preposition and is weak here: /fə/. The /k/ of “ask” links onto it, and before the vowel of “it” a linking /r/ appears in the British model: “as-kuh-rit”. So a weak form and two links share one tiny stretch. Spotting both lets you decode the stretch.
quests.phoneticRule: A weak function word between two content words receives the preceding consonant by linking and passes a linking /r/ to a following vowel.

quests.instruction: In “for us” in “Dario, wait for us outside”, which part is the linking /r/ and which is the weak form?
quests.word: Dario, wait for us outside
quests.textToSpeak: Dario, wait for us outside
options: The /r/ is a weak form of “us”, and the vowels link them together
The /r/ and both vowels are weak forms, so nothing is linked at all between the two words
Both words are strong, and the /r/ is simply an extra sound
The /r/ joins “for” to “us” (linking), and both words are reduced to /fər/ and /əs/
quests.correctAnswer: The /r/ joins “for” to “us” (linking), and both words are reduced to /fər/ and /əs/
quests.hint: Separate the consonant that joins the words from the vowels that have been reduced.
quests.explanation: Two processes overlap. “For” is weak: /fə/ before a consonant, /fər/ before a vowel. The /r/ in /fər/ is the linking /r/ that joins it to “us”. “Us” itself is weak, /əs/. So “fuh-rus” has a linking /r/ plus two reduced vowels. Telling them apart helps you understand what each sound is doing.
quests.phoneticRule: A linking /r/ is a consonant that joins two words, whereas weak forms are reductions of vowels; both can occur in the same chunk.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form fits “Esme, look at it again”?
quests.word: Esme, look at it again
quests.textToSpeak: Esme, look at it again
options: “look … at … it … again”: four strong words with breaks between them
“loo-kə-ti-tagain”: a weak “at”, with the /k/ and two /t/ sounds linked
“loo-at-it-again”: the /k/ and the /t/ sounds are dropped altogether
“loo-kat-it-gain”: “at” is strong and the links are misplaced
quests.correctAnswer: “loo-kə-ti-tagain”: a weak “at”, with the /k/ and two /t/ sounds linked
quests.hint: Count the vowel-initial words and decide which consonant attaches to each.
quests.explanation: “Look” links its /k/ onto the weak “at” (/ət/), the /t/ of “at” links onto “it”, and the /t/ of “it” links onto “again”. The result is a single chain, “loo-kə-ti-tagain”. Recognising the chain helps you understand a short request.
quests.phoneticRule: In a chain of vowel-initial function words, each word's final consonant links to the next, and the vowel of the function word is reduced.

quests.instruction: Which features are heard in “Helen, put my bag on the bench”?
quests.word: Helen, put my bag on the bench
quests.textToSpeak: Helen, put my bag on the bench
options: Assimilation in “put my” (the /t/ shifts to /p/) and linking in “bag on”
Linking in “put my” and assimilation in “bag on”, the other way round
Elision in “put my” and linking in “bag on”, with no change of place
Assimilation in both “put my” and “bag on”, with no linking at all
quests.correctAnswer: Assimilation in “put my” (the /t/ shifts to /p/) and linking in “bag on”
quests.hint: For each boundary ask whether a consonant changes place or simply moves onto a vowel.
quests.explanation: “Put my” has a /t/ before the lip sound /m/, so the /t/ can move to the lips: assimilation. “Bag on” has a /g/ before a vowel, so the /g/ links onto “on”: linking. The sentence therefore shows one change of place and one move. Checking each boundary separately keeps the two ideas apart.
quests.phoneticRule: At each boundary, the next sound decides the process: a consonant of a different place may trigger assimilation, and a vowel triggers linking.

quests.instruction: In “Isaac, sit by me on the train”, which boundary shows assimilation and which a glide link?
quests.word: Isaac, sit by me on the train
quests.textToSpeak: Isaac, sit by me on the train
options: “sit by” shows a glide link, and “me on” shows assimilation of the nasal before a vowel
Both boundaries show assimilation, one at the lips and one at the back
Both boundaries show glide links, one /j/ and one /w/
“sit by” shows assimilation (/t/ toward /p/); “me on” shows a /j/ glide link
quests.correctAnswer: “sit by” shows assimilation (/t/ toward /p/); “me on” shows a /j/ glide link
quests.hint: Check what ends and begins each pair: a consonant before a lip sound, or a vowel before a vowel.
quests.explanation: “Sit” ends in /t/ and “by” begins with /b/, so the /t/ can move to the lips. “Me” ends in a vowel and “on” begins with one, so a light /j/ glide links them. Two different boundary types appear in the same short sentence, and each is handled by a different process.
quests.phoneticRule: Consonant + consonant boundaries may trigger assimilation, while vowel + vowel boundaries trigger glides.
quests.spokenForm: Isaac, sip by me-yon the train

quests.instruction: Which spoken form fits “Jules, turn back and ask me”?
quests.word: Jules, turn back and ask me
quests.textToSpeak: Jules, turn back and ask me
options: “turn back and ask me”, with every sound unchanged and separate from the next
“turm ba-kən ask me”: assimilation in “turn back”, linking in “back and”
“tur back an ask me”, with the /n/ dropped in “turn” altogether
“turn bak-and-ask-me”, with the /k/ moved onto the word “ask”
quests.correctAnswer: “turm ba-kən ask me”: assimilation in “turn back”, linking in “back and”
quests.hint: Spot the nasal before a lip sound, then the consonant before a vowel.
quests.explanation: The /n/ of “turn” sits before /b/, so it can shift to [m]: “turm back”. The /k/ of “back” sits before the weak “and”, so it links: “ba-kən”. Both processes occur in one clause, and neither affects the other.
quests.phoneticRule: Assimilation and linking can occur in adjacent boundaries without interfering, so a chunk may contain both.

quests.instruction: What happens to the /t/ of “just” in “Karim, just ask her about it”, and why?
quests.word: Karim, just ask her about it
quests.textToSpeak: Karim, just ask her about it
options: It is omitted, because a /t/ after /s/ is always omitted in speech
It links onto “ask”, because a vowel follows, so it is kept
It becomes a /k/ to match the /k/ of “ask” that follows it
It blends with “her” into /tʃ/ across the two words
quests.correctAnswer: It links onto “ask”, because a vowel follows, so it is kept
quests.hint: Look at the sound that follows the /t/. Is it a consonant or a vowel?
quests.explanation: “Just” ends in /st/, and “ask” begins with a vowel, so the /t/ has a vowel to link onto: “jus-task”. Elision would need a consonant after the /t/, as in “just call”. So the same word has two possible outcomes, decided by the next sound. In the same sentence “ask her” also links: “as-ker”.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final /t/ after /s/ links before a vowel, and omission is possible only before a consonant.

quests.instruction: Compare “just ask” with “just call”. What changes in “Lucy, just call her tonight”?
quests.word: Lucy, just call her tonight
quests.textToSpeak: Lucy, just call her tonight
options: A consonant follows the /t/, so it is often omitted: “jus’ call”
The /t/ is followed by a vowel, so it links onto the next word as in “jus-tcall”
The /t/ blends with the /k/ into a completely new sound
The /t/ moves onto “call” unchanged, as in “jus-tcall”
quests.correctAnswer: A consonant follows the /t/, so it is often omitted: “jus’ call”
quests.hint: Compare the first sound of “ask” with the first sound of “call”.
quests.explanation: “Call” begins with a consonant, so the /t/ of “just” is again in a crowded spot and is often left out: “jus’ call”. In “just ask” it was followed by a vowel and linked. The difference in the next sound is the whole explanation.
quests.phoneticRule: The same word-final /t/ is retained and linked before a vowel but may be omitted before a consonant.

quests.instruction: Which boundaries show elision and which show linking in “Marco, my best friend asked her”?
quests.word: Marco, my best friend asked her
quests.textToSpeak: Marco, my best friend asked her
options: Linking in “best friend”, and elision in “friend asked”, the other way round from what happens
Elision at both boundaries, with the /t/ and the /d/ both omitted
Linking at both boundaries, with the /t/ and the /d/ both moved
Elision in “best friend” (the /t/ is omitted), linking in “friend asked” (the /d/ moves)
quests.correctAnswer: Elision in “best friend” (the /t/ is omitted), linking in “friend asked” (the /d/ moves)
quests.hint: Check what follows each word-final consonant: a consonant or a vowel.
quests.explanation: “Best” ends in /st/ before the consonant /f/, so the /t/ is often omitted. “Friend” ends in /nd/ before the vowel of “asked”, so the /d/ links onto it. Applying the rule to each boundary gives “bes’ fren-dasked”.
quests.phoneticRule: Elision and linking are decided boundary by boundary: consonant + consonant allows omission, consonant + vowel gives linking.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form fits “Petra, how could you forget?”
quests.word: Petra, how could you forget
quests.textToSpeak: Petra, how could you forget
options: “how cou-ja forget”: /d/ + /j/ blend into /dʒ/, with a weak “you”
“how could you forget”: three strong words with a clear /j/
“how cou-cha forget”: the blend is /tʃ/ with a weak “you”
“how coo-ya forget”: the /d/ is dropped before the weak “you”
quests.correctAnswer: “how cou-ja forget”: /d/ + /j/ blend into /dʒ/, with a weak “you”
quests.hint: Look at the end of “could” and the start of “you”, then decide how strong “you” is.
quests.explanation: “Could” ends in /d/ and “you” is weak, /jə/. The two blend into /dʒ/: “cou-ja”. Emotional questions are said quickly, and the blend plus the weak “you” makes the phrase easy to miss. Hearing /dʒə/ should bring “could you” to mind.
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescence and weak-form reduction combine in questions: /d/ + weak /jə/ gives /dʒə/.

quests.instruction: Which sentence matches the quick “Sofia, di-ja te-ləm yet?”
quests.word: Sofia, did you tell them yet
quests.textToSpeak: Sofia, did you tell them yet
options: “Sofia, did you tell him yet?”
“Sofia, did you tell them yet?”
“Sofia, would you tell them yet?”
“Sofia, did she tell them yet?”
quests.correctAnswer: “Sofia, did you tell them yet?”
quests.hint: Check the vowel in the last syllable of “te-ləm”, and the sound at the start of the second word.
quests.explanation: “Di-ja” points to “did you” (/d/ + /j/ → /dʒ/). “Te-ləm” has a schwa before the /m/, which fits weak “them” (/əm/); “him” would be /ɪm/. “Would you” would begin with a /w/, and “did she” has no /j/. The details decide the match.
quests.phoneticRule: Decoding a fast sentence uses several cues together: the blend identifies “you”, and the reduced vowel separates “them” from “him”.

quests.instruction: Which features are heard in “Ulla, pass your coat to me”?
quests.word: Ulla, pass your coat to me
quests.textToSpeak: Ulla, pass your coat to me
options: A /ʃ/ blend in “pass your”, a weak “your”, and a weak “to”
A /ʒ/ blend in “pass your”, with a strong “to” before “me”
No blend, because “pass” ends in a vowel sound
A /tʃ/ blend in “pass your”, with a strong “your” as well
quests.correctAnswer: A /ʃ/ blend in “pass your”, a weak “your”, and a weak “to”
quests.hint: Name the last sound of “pass”, then check the small words “your” and “to”.
quests.explanation: “Pass” ends in /s/, so with /j/ it blends into /ʃ/. “Your” is weak (/jə/), and “to” is weak (/tə/): “pa-shyer coat tuh me”. The same sentence thus combines coalescence with two weak forms.
quests.phoneticRule: A weak “your” triggers the blend, and the sentence's other function words are reduced independently.

quests.instruction: How many syllables does “she’d’ve” have in “Wendy said she’d’ve come”?
quests.word: Wendy said she’d’ve come
quests.textToSpeak: Wendy said she’d’ve come
options: Three: /ʃiː wʊd həv/, with a full “would have” spoken in full
One: /ʃiːv/, with the /d/ lost completely from the contraction
Four: /ʃiː hæd əv/, with a full “had of” spoken in full
Two: /ʃiːdəv/, with “’d’ve” squeezed into one weak syllable
quests.correctAnswer: Two: /ʃiːdəv/, with “’d’ve” squeezed into one weak syllable
quests.hint: Say “she’d’ve” aloud and count the beats.
quests.explanation: “She’d’ve” stands for “she would have”, and it is pronounced as two syllables: /ʃiːdəv/. The “’d’ve” part is a single weak syllable. This double contraction is a spoken form and is rarely written in formal text, but it is very common in conversation.
quests.phoneticRule: Double contractions such as “’d’ve” compress two function words into one weak syllable, /dəv/.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “wouldn’t’ve” fits “Xavier wouldn’t’ve known”?
quests.word: Xavier wouldn’t’ve known
quests.textToSpeak: Xavier wouldn’t’ve known
options: “would not have”: three strong words, one after the other
“wood-ntəv”: a syllabic /n/ followed by a weak “’ve”
“woodn-tov”: a full /ɒv/ ending on the last syllable of the word
“woodnt-have”: a strong “have” with a clear /h/ sound at the start
quests.correctAnswer: “wood-ntəv”: a syllabic /n/ followed by a weak “’ve”
quests.hint: Remember the two reductions you have studied: the syllabic /n/ and the weak “’ve”.
quests.explanation: “Wouldn’t’ve” combines two reductions: the syllabic /n/ of “wouldn’t” and the weak /əv/ of “’ve”. The result is a compact /ˈwʊdntəv/. The /t/ links onto the weak vowel. The form is informal, but recognising it helps with fast conversation.
quests.phoneticRule: Stacked contractions combine earlier patterns: a syllabic /n/ followed by a /t/ that links onto weak /əv/.

quests.instruction: Which reductions are heard in “Viktor said we’re going to be late”?
quests.word: Viktor said we’re going to be late
quests.textToSpeak: Viktor said we’re going to be late
options: Only a contraction; “going to” is unchanged and fully pronounced
Only “gonna”; “we’re” is two full words, “we are”
A contraction (“we’re”) and the informal “gonna” for “going to”
Elision of “be” and a strong “late” that carries no stress
quests.correctAnswer: A contraction (“we’re”) and the informal “gonna” for “going to”
quests.hint: List the small reductions you know: contractions, weak forms and the informal forms.
quests.explanation: “We’re” is a standard contraction, and “going to” is often said as the informal “gonna”. Both appear in the same short clause. The words “be late” keep their stress, so the clause still has a clear rhythm.
quests.phoneticRule: Standard contractions and informal reductions combine in casual speech and are recognised independently.
quests.spokenForm: Viktor sed we’re gonna be late

quests.instruction: Which features are heard in “Fatima, ask him if he’s coming”?
quests.word: Fatima, ask him if he’s coming
quests.textToSpeak: Fatima, ask him if he’s coming
options: Dropped /h/ in “him” and “he’s”, with “ask” and “if” linking on
Clear /h/ sounds in both words, with a pause before each one of the pronouns
A dropped /h/ in “him” only, and a clear /h/ in “he’s”
Glides instead of links in both places, with the /h/ kept
quests.correctAnswer: Dropped /h/ in “him” and “he’s”, with “ask” and “if” linking on
quests.hint: Find the two pronouns and notice what the consonants before them do.
quests.explanation: Both pronouns follow a word and are unstressed, so their /h/ is dropped. The /k/ of “ask” links onto “him” (“as-kim”), and the /f/ of “if” links onto “he’s” (“i-fiz”). Two instances of the same pattern appear in one sentence.
quests.phoneticRule: Unstressed pronouns drop /h/ after another word, and the final consonant of the preceding word links onto the resulting vowel-initial form.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form fits “Gus has had his lunch”?
quests.word: Gus has had his lunch
quests.textToSpeak: Gus has had his lunch
options: “HAS HAD HIS”: all three are strong, with clear /h/ sounds
“həz-əd-iz”: “has”, “had” and “his” are weak, with no /h/ after “Gus”
“has had iz”: only “his” is weak, and the others keep their /h/ and their strong vowels
“Gus az ad hiz”: only the last /h/ is kept, in “his”
quests.correctAnswer: “həz-əd-iz”: “has”, “had” and “his” are weak, with no /h/ after “Gus”
quests.hint: Look at the three words after “Gus” and decide which are stressed and which are only grammar.
quests.explanation: In “Gus has had his lunch”, the stressed words are “Gus” and “lunch”. The words “has”, “had” and “his” are all unstressed, so each is weak and drops its /h/: “həz əd iz”. Three /h/ sounds disappear in a row, which is why the phrase can be hard to follow at first.
quests.phoneticRule: A sequence of unstressed /h/-initial function words loses every /h/, giving a run of weak vowel-initial syllables.

quests.instruction: In “Cleo, have you seen her?”, which /h/ is most likely to be dropped in fast, standard speech?
quests.word: Cleo, have you seen her
quests.textToSpeak: Cleo, have you seen her
options: The /h/ of “have”, because it is an auxiliary verb
Both /h/ sounds equally, because both are in unstressed words
Neither: the /h/ is kept in every position in the sentence
The /h/ of “her”, because it follows “seen” and is unstressed
quests.correctAnswer: The /h/ of “her”, because it follows “seen” and is unstressed
quests.hint: Think about which /h/ follows another word and which begins the question.
quests.explanation: “Have” begins the question, so it keeps its /h/. “Her” follows “seen” and is unstressed, so it drops its /h/: “see-nər”. So position and stress decide which /h/ goes. The same sentence therefore contains one kept /h/ and one dropped /h/.
quests.phoneticRule: Initial position protects /h/, while a following unstressed position allows it to drop.

quests.instruction: Which features are heard in “Quentin, add some more eggs”?
quests.word: Quentin, add some more eggs
quests.textToSpeak: Quentin, add some more eggs
options: Two separate /m/ sounds, and no link before “eggs” at all in the phrase
A dropped /m/, and a /w/ glide before “eggs” instead
A held /m/ in “some more”, and a linking /r/ before “eggs”
A held /m/, and a /j/ glide before “eggs” instead
quests.correctAnswer: A held /m/ in “some more”, and a linking /r/ before “eggs”
quests.hint: Look at the two boundaries: identical consonants, then a spelled “r” before a vowel.
quests.explanation: “Some” ends in /m/ and “more” begins with /m/, so the lips hold one longer /m/. “More” ends in a spelled “r” and “eggs” begins with a vowel, so a linking /r/ appears: “mo-reggs”. So gemination and linking /r/ sit side by side.
quests.phoneticRule: Gemination at one boundary and linking /r/ at the next can occur within the same three-word chunk.

quests.instruction: Which description fits “Nadia, take that time off”?
quests.word: Nadia, take that time off
quests.textToSpeak: Nadia, take that time off
options: “that time” has two clear /t/ sounds, and “time off” is separated
“tha-time” drops the /t/ entirely, and “off” is stressed
“that time” has one held /t/, and the /m/ of “time” links onto “off”
“that-ttime” has three /t/ sounds in a row before “off”
quests.correctAnswer: “that time” has one held /t/, and the /m/ of “time” links onto “off”
quests.hint: Check each boundary: identical consonants first, then a consonant before a vowel.
quests.explanation: “That” and “time” meet at /t/ + /t/, so one longer /t/ is held. “Time” ends in /m/ before the vowel of “off”, so the /m/ links: “ti-moff”. The result is “tha-ttime-moff”, one smooth chunk.
quests.phoneticRule: A held consonant at one boundary does not prevent linking at the next boundary.

quests.instruction: Which features are heard in “Ravi, hot tea is ready”?
quests.word: Ravi, hot tea is ready
quests.textToSpeak: Ravi, hot tea is ready
options: Two separate /t/ sounds, and a /w/ glide before “is”
A dropped /t/, and a linking /r/ before “is”
One held /t/, and a linking /r/ before “is”
One held /t/ in “hot tea”, and a /j/ glide before “is”
quests.correctAnswer: One held /t/ in “hot tea”, and a /j/ glide before “is”
quests.hint: Remember that “tea” ends in a high front vowel before the vowel of “is”.
quests.explanation: “Hot” ends in /t/ and “tea” begins with /t/, so one closure is held. “Tea” ends in /iː/ and “is” begins with a vowel, so a /j/ glide appears: “ho-ttea-yis”. No /r/ is possible because “tea” has no spelled “r”.
quests.phoneticRule: Gemination and glide linking can occur in the same short sentence, each decided by its own boundary.

quests.instruction: In many non-rhotic accents, an /r/ appears in “idea of” even without a spelled “r”. Which spoken form fits “Wendy, I like the idea of it”?
quests.word: Wendy, I like the idea of it
quests.textToSpeak: Wendy, I like the idea of it
options: “idea-wof”: a /w/ glide is inserted instead
“idea-jof”: a /j/ glide is inserted instead
“idea-rof”: an /r/ is inserted between the two vowels
“idea-of”: the vowels must stay separate in every accent
quests.correctAnswer: “idea-rof”: an /r/ is inserted between the two vowels
quests.hint: This /r/ is not in the spelling. Think about the vowel at the end of “idea”.
quests.explanation: In non-rhotic accents like General British, the linking /r/ after a spelled “r” (far away) has spread by analogy to words ending in /ə/, /ɑː/ or /ɔː/ without an “r”, such as “idea of” or “law and”. This is called intrusive /r/. It is common in speech in many British accents, but it is absent in rhotic accents and some speakers avoid it in careful speech. Recognising it matters more than producing it.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive /r/ is an /r/ inserted after /ə/, /ɑː/ or /ɔː/ before a vowel-initial word in non-rhotic accents, even without a spelled “r”; it is accent-dependent and optional.
quests.spokenForm: Wendy, I like the idea-rof it

quests.instruction: Which boundary in “Xavier, saw it and left” can have an intrusive /r/?
quests.word: Xavier, saw it and left
quests.textToSpeak: Xavier, saw it and left
options: “it and”, because “it” ends in /t/, and any final consonant can take an /r/
“and left”, because “and” ends in /d/, which can take an /r/
None: an /r/ needs a spelled “r”, so “saw it” cannot have one
“saw it”: “saw” ends in /ɔː/ and “it” starts with a vowel
quests.correctAnswer: “saw it”: “saw” ends in /ɔː/ and “it” starts with a vowel
quests.hint: Look for a word that ends in a vowel such as /ɔː/ and is followed by a vowel-initial word.
quests.explanation: “Saw” ends in /ɔː/ and “it” begins with a vowel, which is exactly the setting for an intrusive /r/ in non-rhotic accents: “saw-rit”. The boundaries “it and” and “and left” involve consonants, which link instead. The idea that an /r/ needs a spelled “r” holds for linking /r/, but not for intrusive /r/.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive /r/ is restricted to vowel + vowel boundaries after /ə/, /ɑː/ or /ɔː/; consonant-final words link unchanged instead.

quests.instruction: In a non-rhotic accent, which form is typical for “pizza and” in “Yusuf, pizza and pasta are ready”?
quests.word: Yusuf, pizza and pasta are ready
quests.textToSpeak: Yusuf, pizza and pasta are ready
options: “pizza-wand”: a /w/ glide appears after the final vowel of “pizza”
“pizz-and”: the final vowel is dropped before “and”
“pizza-rand”: an /r/ is common (but optional) after final /ə/
“pizza-rand” occurs only in American English
quests.correctAnswer: “pizza-rand”: an /r/ is common (but optional) after final /ə/
quests.hint: Think of the vowel at the end of “pizza”, and remember that this pattern is optional.
quests.explanation: “Pizza” ends in /ə/, and “and” begins with a vowel, so many non-rhotic speakers insert an /r/: “pizza-rand”. It is common but optional, and rhotic accents do not use it. Since “pasta are” has the same shape, you may hear two intrusive /r/ sounds in one sentence.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive /r/ also follows word-final /ə/ in words such as “pizza” and “China”, in accents that use it.

quests.instruction: Which feature is most likely to make a learner fail to recognise “did you” in “Gus, did you eat it all?”
quests.word: Gus, did you eat it all
quests.textToSpeak: Gus, did you eat it all
options: The linking /t/ in “eat it”, because it moves a sound onto the next word
The /dʒ/ blend, because it replaces two familiar sounds with a new one
The weak “it”, because it is short and quiet in the sentence
The stress on “eat”, because it comes first in the clause
quests.correctAnswer: The /dʒ/ blend, because it replaces two familiar sounds with a new one
quests.hint: Think about which change makes a familiar word sound like a different word.
quests.explanation: A linked /t/ or a weak vowel moves or shortens a sound, but the word is still recognisable. The blend /dʒ/ replaces /d/ + /j/ with a new sound, so “did you” sounds like “dija”. That makes the blend the most likely to hide the words. Knowing it helps you decode them.
quests.phoneticRule: Features that substitute a new sound (coalescence) obscure words more than features that merely move or shorten sounds (linking, weak forms).

quests.instruction: In “Cleo, I’d’ve asked him”, which feature most changes the sound compared with the written words?
quests.word: Cleo, I’d’ve asked him
quests.textToSpeak: Cleo, I’d’ve asked him
options: The link in “asked him”, which only moves a /k/ onto the next vowel in the phrase
The stress on “asked”, which is a normal beat in the sentence
The contraction “I’d’ve”, which squeezes three words into two syllables
The name “Cleo”, which is a vocative at the start
quests.correctAnswer: The contraction “I’d’ve”, which squeezes three words into two syllables
quests.hint: Compare how many written words and how many spoken syllables each option represents.
quests.explanation: “I’d’ve” stands for “I would have”, three written words that are said as two quick weak syllables: /aɪdəv/. That is a bigger difference from the written form than the link in “asked him”. Spotting the double contraction is therefore the key to decoding the sentence.
quests.phoneticRule: Double contractions create the largest gap between spelling and sound, because they compress several words into very few syllables.

quests.instruction: In “Zara, the idea is great”, which feature adds a sound that is not in the spelling?
quests.word: Zara, the idea is great
quests.textToSpeak: Zara, the idea is great
options: The intrusive /r/ in “idea is”, which appears between two vowels
The weak “the”, which is simply shortened to a short vowel
The stress on “great”, which is a normal beat in the sentence
The linking of “is”, which only moves a /z/ onto the next word
quests.correctAnswer: The intrusive /r/ in “idea is”, which appears between two vowels
quests.hint: Check which option inserts a consonant that is not written.
quests.explanation: Weak forms and stress shorten or lengthen existing sounds, and the linking of “is” moves a /z/ that is already there. The intrusive /r/ in “idea-ris” adds a new /r/ with no letter behind it. That is why it stands out to learners reading and listening. It is accent-dependent and optional.
quests.phoneticRule: Intrusive /r/ inserts a consonant with no letter or underlying sound behind it, in contrast with weak forms and stress, which only modify existing sounds.

quests.instruction: Which features are heard in “Isaac, I’d’ve asked her last night”?
quests.word: Isaac, I’d’ve asked her last night
quests.textToSpeak: Isaac, I’d’ve asked her last night
options: A contraction (“I’d’ve”), a dropped /h/ with a link, and elision in “last night”
Coalescence in “asked her”, plus a strong “I’d’ve” in full
Assimilation in “last night”, plus an intrusive /r/ after “asked” and before “her”
Gemination in “last night”, plus a /j/ glide in “asked her”
quests.correctAnswer: A contraction (“I’d’ve”), a dropped /h/ with a link, and elision in “last night”
quests.hint: Go through the sentence in order and name one feature for each of the three stretches.
quests.explanation: “I’d’ve” is a double contraction, “asked her” has a dropped /h/ with the /t/ linking onto the weak “her”, and “last night” has an omitted /t/ before /n/. So one sentence combines three different features, each at its own boundary. The more of them you can name, the more of the sentence you can decode.
quests.phoneticRule: Realistic sentences combine several connected-speech features, each decided by its own boundary and context.

quests.instruction: Which features are heard in “Jules, did you tell him yet?”
quests.word: Jules, did you tell him yet
quests.textToSpeak: Jules, did you tell him yet
options: Elision of the /d/, and a /j/ glide before “you”
Assimilation of the /d/, and a strong “him” with a clear /h/
A /dʒ/ blend (“did you”), and a dropped /h/ linked to “tell”
A /tʃ/ blend, and gemination in “tell him” across the words
quests.correctAnswer: A /dʒ/ blend (“did you”), and a dropped /h/ linked to “tell”
quests.hint: Name the process at “did you” and the process at “tell him”.
quests.explanation: “Did you” blends into /dʒ/, and “him” loses its /h/ so the /l/ of “tell” links onto it: “di-ja te-lim yet”. The final “yet” begins with /j/, but “him” ends in /m/, which does not blend, so “him yet” stays clear. Two different features appear in one question.
quests.phoneticRule: Coalescence applies only to /t d s z/ + /j/, so “him yet” keeps its /j/ even though the next word begins with it.

quests.instruction: Which features are heard in “Karim, I’m going to get you some more tea”?
quests.word: Karim, I’m going to get you some more tea
quests.textToSpeak: Karim, I’m going to get you some more tea
options: A reduction (“gonna”), a /tʃ/ blend (“get you”), and a held /m/ (“some more”)
A contraction, an elision of /t/ in “get you”, and a linking /r/
A weak “to”, a /dʒ/ blend and a dropped /h/ in “you”
Assimilation of /n/ in “gonna”, gemination in “get you” and elision in “more tea”
quests.correctAnswer: A reduction (“gonna”), a /tʃ/ blend (“get you”), and a held /m/ (“some more”)
quests.hint: Move through the sentence from left to right and name the feature at each stretch.
quests.explanation: “Going to” is reduced to “gonna”, “get you” blends into /tʃ/, and “some more” holds one /m/. Each belongs to a different stage of this course: reduction, coalescence and gemination. Hearing all three at once is the sign that you can follow natural speech.
quests.phoneticRule: A single realistic sentence can combine reduction, coalescence and gemination, each triggered by its own sounds.
quests.spokenForm: Karim, I’m gonna ge-choo summore tea
